extracted.intended_audience: general readers of Montaigne; students of literature and readers interested in reflections on war, fame, and horsemanship
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading of translated essays by Michel de Montaigne (chapters on fame, uncertainty of judgment, and war-horses), extracting prescriptive observations and practical principles embedded in the prose. Suitable for literary study or for extracting early-modern practical/philosophical guidance about warfare and reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursue victory promptly
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Tis not here, as in fencing, where the most hits gain the prize; for so long as the enemy is on foot, the game is new to begin, and that is not to be called a victory that puts not an end to the war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a victory does not finish the war, its utility is limited; seize the moment while fortune is fresh (quoting Lucan: 'Dum fortuna calet, dum conficit omnia terror'). Examples and critiques include missed opportunities at Moncontour and St. Quentin; Caesar reproaching Pompey's officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise restraint after victory
rubrics_metrics.description: To throw a man's self into danger after a victory obtained is again to expose himself to the mercy of fortune; it is sometimes one of the greatest discretions in the rule of war not to press a victory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance the impulse to pursue with the risk of overreaching: examples include Sylla and Marius refraining against desperate reserves, Monsieur de Foix whose ardour cost him his life, and Monsieur d'Anguien who learned from that example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid driving the enemy to despair
rubrics_metrics.description: It is one of the greatest discretions in the rule of war not to drive an enemy to despair; necessity teaches violent resolutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forcing an enemy into desperate measures can produce fiercer resistance; historical examples (Marsians, Pharax's decision to let defeated foes escape, Clodomir’s pursuit costing his life) illustrate the danger of provoking resolute counteraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider psychological effects of soldiers' equipment
rubrics_metrics.description: Sumptuous or brave attire can enflame courage and serve as a spur, yet great booty and rich equipage may tempt soldiers and encourage avarice and indiscipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh morale benefits of fine equipment (Sertorius, Philopcem, Brutus, Caesar) against the increased temptation to flee or plunder and the enemy's motivation (Antiochus/Hannibal anecdote). Lycurgus’ prohibition on finery is cited as the opposite policy to preserve discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use insults and denial of quarter cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: At sieges and elsewhere, taking from the enemy all hopes of mercy by injurious language can be of consequence to force them to fight; but taunts can also stiffen enemy resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne notes both the rationale for representing that no fair quarter will be expected and the counterexample of Vitellius, whose reproaches enlivened Otho's troops; therefore, such tactics are double-edged and should be used with caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: General's visibility vs disguise (leader presence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Changing habit and disguising the person of a general may preserve his life but deprive his men of morale; conversely, conspicuous leaders inspire troops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Pyrrhus disguised preserved his life but nearly lost the battle by losing soldiers' confidence; Alexander, Caesar, and Lucullus favored being known in battle, while Agis and Agesilaus fought obscurely. Choose based on tradeoffs between personal safety and leadership presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose formation and motion relative to enemy posture
rubrics_metrics.description: If your enemy comes full drive upon you, stand firm to receive him; if he stands to receive you, run full drive upon him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactical rule illustrated by Clearchus’s measured advance (soft approach then sudden rush) and other examples: match your manoeuvre to the opponent’s momentum to preserve order while gaining the advantage of impetuosity or steadiness as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh defending home territory versus attacking abroad
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to defend one's dominions or to carry the war into enemy lands by considering supplies, local support, ambush risk, and long-term advantages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pros of defending: supply, affection of subjects, fortified cities, ability to choose the time of battle; cons: enemy may find advantage in hostile country. Examples: Charles V. into Provence, Scipio attacking Africa successfully, Hannibal ruined by defending home, Athenians in Sicily failing vs Agathocles' success in Africa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer weapons you can control (short weapons over firearms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose weapons of the shortest sort and those you can best account for; a man himself strikes surer than a bullet discharged from a pistol which depends on powder, flint, and mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne advises confidence in the sword over pistols due to mechanical failure risks; the sword's directness and reliability in close combat argued as superior to early firearms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize advantages and limits of missile weapons and engines
rubrics_metrics.description: Ancient missile weapons (Phalarica, slings, darts, siege engines) and modern cannon can be terrible and thunderous, but in close fight they may harm attackers and provoke dislike in certain peoples favoring hand-to-hand combat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Italians’ Phalarica (burning darts), slingers’ precision from Livy, Dionysius’s engines approximating modern artillery, and the Gauls’ abhorrence for treacherous missile arms—use depending on context and expected effects in open vs close combat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain fresh mounts (use destriers/funales)
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep led horses (funales/destrarios) or fresh mounts available to change upon in battle so riders can mount fresh horses as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Romans and Numidians practiced changing mounts to maintain speed and endurance; the term 'destriers' used for service horses and desultorii equi (horses trained for desultory mounting) are historical practices for sustaining cavalry effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious training horses to attack automatically
rubrics_metrics.description: Horses trained to attack on command can fall upon enemies but often do more harm to friends and cannot be easily recalled when grappled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Risk illustrated by Artybius’s death when his trained horse was mortally wounded; such animals may be useful but bring the danger of friendly casualties and loss of control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer fighting on foot for steadiness and mutual accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Battles fought on foot stake soldiers’ valour and fortune on themselves rather than their horses; such fights were more firm and furious in former times compared to modern routs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues ancestors often fought on foot to rely on personal courage and constancy; the image given: victors and vanquished falling pell-mell with little flight—contrasted with modern emphasis on cavalry and routs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge the role of fortune in counsel and events
rubrics_metrics.description: Our councils and deliberations depend as much upon fortune as anything else we do; arguments and decisions partake in the temerity of chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting Timaeus and Manilius, Montaigne stresses that prudence and reason are subject to caprice and chance; decision-makers should therefore recognize uncertainty and be humble about supposed control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fame and names are arbitrary and unstable
rubrics_metrics.description: Fame often rests on sound, letters, or accident (a name's orthography) rather than intrinsic worth; the glory attached to a name may be transported or assumed by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Denisot’s anagram inventing Count d’Alsinois, Suetonius changing Lenis to Tranquillus, multiple historical figures sharing the same distinguished names; Montaigne questions to whom the glory truly belongs and highlights fame's fragility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputation does not profit the dead; survivors project feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: Survivors flatter the dead with verses and praise, attributing to them the survivors’ own feelings and hopes, though the dead neither regard nor benefit from such renown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne cites the Aeneid ('Id cinerem et manes credis curare sepultos?') and notes that survivors comfort themselves by projecting their desires, implying fame is more solace for the living than real advantage for the dead.
